entries.name: Romans
entries.region: Italy, then the whole Mediterranean world
entries.settlement: walled cities laid on a grid, a forum and aqueduct at the centre
trade: grain in from Egypt and Sicily
tin and amber from the north
silk and spices via the east
entries.beliefs: state gods (Jupiter, Juno, Mars) with household and ancestor cults; later Christianity
entries.fell_by: internal division, plague and Germanic invasion; the Western Empire collapsed in 476 CE
entries.notes: The template empire: law, roads, concrete and citizenship carried by the legions. Half of the game's building ids descend from them.

entries.name: Greeks
entries.region: Greece, the Aegean, Asia Minor and colonies around the Mediterranean and Black Sea
entries.settlement: independent city-states (poleis) with an agora and a fortified acropolis
entries.beliefs: Olympian gods led by Zeus; oracles, mystery cults, city patron deities
entries.fell_by: endless city-state rivalry (Peloponnesian War), then Roman conquest (146 BCE); culture survived inside Rome
entries.notes: Coined citizenship, philosophy, theatre and the Olympic games; every Mediterranean people measured itself against them.

entries.name: Athenians
entries.settlement: one large polis around the Acropolis, with the port at Piraeus
entries.beliefs: Athena as patron of the polis; civic religion bound to citizenship
entries.fell_by: defeat in the Peloponnesian War (404 BCE), then Macedonian overrule after Chaeronea (338 BCE)
entries.notes: The radical democracy of the assembly and the jury-court; direct ancestor of modern civic institutions.

entries.name: Spartans
entries.settlement: five unwalled villages; barracks, gym and communal mess halls (syssitia) instead of city walls
entries.beliefs: Apollo and Ares; oracle at Delphi; royal ancestor cult around Lycurgus
entries.fell_by: helot revolts and defeat at Leuctra (371 BCE); Sparta lingered passively until Rome absorbed Greece
entries.notes: A warrior aristocracy raised by the agoge; the 300 at Thermopylae made them the enduring image of discipline.

entries.name: Macedonians
entries.settlement: loosely unified kingdom of upland cantons under an Argead king
crafts: sarissa pike phalanx and siege engines
entries.beliefs: Greek Olympian pantheon; royal ancestor cult of the Argead house
entries.fell_by: defeat by Rome at Pydna (168 BCE); the kingdom abolished and split into four republics
entries.notes: Alexander's conquest carried Greek culture to India; Hellenistic civilisation outlived the kingdom by centuries.

entries.name: Carthaginians
entries.region: North Africa (Tunisia), with colonies in Iberia, Sicily, Sardinia and Malta
subsistence: grain and orchards of the Bagradas valley
entries.settlement: walled port-city of Carthage with a military harbour (the cothon); colonies ringing the western sea
entries.beliefs: Baal Hammon and Tanit; city-god Melqart; tophet child sacrifice (interpretation debated)
entries.fell_by: the three Punic Wars against Rome; the city was destroyed and its site declared cursed in 146 BCE
entries.notes: Rome's great rival for the western Mediterranean; their collision decided who would inherit the sea.

entries.name: Etruscans
entries.settlement: a league of twelve city-states, ruled first by kings then by aristocracies
crafts: the arch and the true vault
trade: Greek pottery and eastern luxury goods in
entries.beliefs: ancestor worship; haruspicy (reading entrails); richly furnished tombs for the afterlife
entries.fell_by: Roman conquest, 4th-3rd century BCE; language faded away by the 1st century CE
entries.notes: Rome borrowed the arch, the toga and gladiatorial games from them; even its first kings were Etruscan.

entries.name: Phoenicians
entries.region: The Levant (modern Lebanon and coastal Syria)
entries.settlement: independent harbour cities (Tyre, Sidon, Byblos); colonies across the western sea
crafts: the alphabet (ancestor of Greek and Latin scripts)
entries.beliefs: Baal and Astarte; city gods Melqart and Eshmun; household and ancestor cults
entries.fell_by: Assyrian, Babylonian, Persian and finally Alexander's conquest of Tyre (332 BCE); Punic colonies taken by Rome
entries.notes: They carried the alphabet around the sea; 'Phoenician' means 'the purple people'.

entries.name: Minoans
entries.settlement: unwalled palace complexes (Knossos, Phaistos) with towns clustered around them
entries.beliefs: bull-leaping ritual and the labrys; a great goddess and her youthful son or consort
entries.fell_by: destruction of the palaces c. 1450 BCE (Thera eruption and Mycenaean takeover); Crete then Mycenaeanised and faded
entries.notes: Europe's first literate civilisation; Linear A is still undeciphered, so every name above survives only in Greek myth.

entries.name: Mycenaeans
entries.settlement: fortified hilltop citadels with megaron palaces; Linear B palace administration
entries.beliefs: early Olympian pantheon recorded in Linear B; hero cult after death
entries.fell_by: the collapse of the Bronze Age c. 1200-1100 BCE (climate, migration, war?); a Greek Dark Age followed
entries.notes: The world of the Trojan War epic; the last literate Bronze Age civilisation before the Greek Dark Age.

entries.name: Egyptians
entries.region: The Nile valley (Egypt), with Nubia and the eastern Mediterranean
entries.settlement: a pharaoh-ruled territorial state divided into nomes; capitals at Memphis and Thebes
entries.beliefs: the divine pharaoh; Ra, Osiris, Isis and the order of Ma'at; an elaborate afterlife cult
entries.fell_by: successive conquests - Assyrians, Persians, Alexander (332 BCE), Ptolemaic kings, then Rome (30 BCE)
entries.notes: The longest-lived literate civilisation on Earth; Rome drank its grain and stole its obelisks.

entries.name: Hittites
entries.settlement: fortified capital Hattusa; a web of vassal kingdoms across Anatolia and north Syria
entries.beliefs: the storm-god Tarhunt and the sun-goddess Arinna; a royal ancestor cult
entries.fell_by: Bronze Age collapse c. 1180 BCE (Sea Peoples, Kaskan raiders, famine); Anatolia fragmented into Neo-Hittite city-states
entries.notes: They met Egypt to a standstill at Kadesh (1274 BCE) and signed the first known peace treaty in history.

entries.name: Gauls
entries.settlement: hillforts (oppida) and open villages; a warrior aristocracy served by a druid priesthood
trade: wine and prestige goods in from Italy
entries.beliefs: druids; gods such as Cernunnos, Lugus and Epona; worship in sacred groves (nemeton)
entries.fell_by: Caesar's conquest (58-50 BCE); the Vercingetorix revolt crushed at Alesia; Gaul was Romanised
entries.notes: They fought Rome for over a century; after Alesia they became the backbone of the Western Empire.

entries.name: Iberians
entries.settlement: fortified hilltop towns (oppida), some covering 20 hectares
crafts: writing in the Northeastern Iberian script
entries.beliefs: fertility goddesses and an Iberian-Greek pantheon; richly furnished warrior tombs
entries.fell_by: Carthaginian then Roman conquest after the Second Punic War; the language was dead by the 2nd century CE
entries.notes: Rome's first battlefield in Iberia (218 BCE); their warriors fought on both sides of the Punic Wars.

entries.name: Celtiberians
entries.settlement: hillforts and walled towns across the Meseta; a fierce warrior society
entries.beliefs: war and ancestor cults; captured Romans were sometimes sacrificed to the gods of victory
entries.fell_by: Roman sieges of Numantia (134-133 BCE); the Celtiberian Wars ended in total defeat
entries.notes: Held out against Rome for two decades; Numantia became Spain's enduring symbol of defiant resistance.

entries.name: Samnites
entries.settlement: villages and hillforts in the Apennines, bound together in the Samnite League
crafts: the samnite fighting style (gladiatorial schools kept it)
entries.beliefs: rustic war gods (Mefitis, Ceres); a warrior aristocracy under hereditary imperia
entries.fell_by: the three Samnite Wars (343-290 BCE); Samnium was absorbed into the Roman Republic
entries.notes: Rome's hardest pre-Hannibal enemy; the Caudine Forks disaster (321 BCE) haunted Rome for a generation.

entries.name: Thracians
entries.settlement: tribal chiefdoms unified loosely in the Odrysian kingdom around the Maritsa river
entries.beliefs: the Thracian horse-hero and Dionysus; Orpheus is their mythical priest-singer
entries.fell_by: conquest by Macedon (357-342 BCE), then Rome took the last Thracian kingdom in 46 CE
entries.notes: Herodotus ranked them second only to India in numbers; Orpheus and Spartacus were both Thracians.

entries.name: Illyrians
entries.region: Illyria (Albania, Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia)
entries.settlement: hillforts (gradina); tribal kings with fleets of fast pirate ships
entries.beliefs: sun and river-god cults; ancestor burial in great tumuli; a fire-god of the sea
entries.fell_by: the Roman Illyrian Wars (229, 219, 168 BCE); king Gentius was captured at Scodra
entries.notes: Rome's first overseas war was against Illyrian pirates; Albanians still regard themselves as their heirs.

entries.name: Dacians
entries.settlement: hilltop fortresses (dava) in the Carpathians, capital Sarmizegetusa Regia
entries.beliefs: Zalmoxis, the god-priest who taught immortality of the soul; priest-kings ruling as semi-divine
entries.fell_by: Trajan's two wars (101-102, 105-106 CE); Sarmizegetusa stormed, Dacia annexed and colonised
entries.notes: Trajan's Column narrates the war; the Dacian treasure fed Rome's great building programme for a generation.

entries.name: Epirotes
entries.settlement: the Molossian tribal state of seventy-plus tribes; later the Epirote league, centred on Dodona
entries.beliefs: Zeus at Dodona, whose will was read in the rustling of the sacred oak and the calls of doves
entries.fell_by: Roman looting of Dodona and conquest after the Third Macedonian War (167 BCE); Epirus annexed
entries.notes: Pyrrhus gave the world the 'pyrrhic victory'; the double-headed eagle of Epirus is Albania's today.

entries.name: Lydians
subsistence: electrum panned from the Pactolus river
entries.settlement: the prosperous city of Sardis; Croesus was the richest man in the Greek imagination
crafts: coinage - the first gold and electrum coins c. 600 BCE
trade: the Royal Road from Sardis to Susa
entries.beliefs: Cybele and Artemis, Anatolian mother-goddesses; the Delphic oracle
entries.fell_by: Cyrus's Persian conquest (546 BCE); Sardis burned; Lydia became a Persian satrapy
entries.notes: They invented money as we know it; 'rich as Croesus' is twenty-five centuries old.

entries.name: Phrygians
entries.settlement: the kingdom of Gordion, capital at Gordion with its great royal tumulus
entries.beliefs: Cybele, the great mother, worshipped at Pessinus; Sabazios, the sky father
entries.fell_by: Cimmerian raids c. 695 BCE; the kingdom shattered and was absorbed by Lydia, then Persia
entries.notes: The Gordian knot was cut by Alexander with a sword; Phrygian may be the closest attested cousin of Greek.

entries.name: Lycians
entries.settlement: rock-valley city-states (Xanthus, Patara) bound together in the Lycian League - a pioneering federation
entries.beliefs: tomb cult and storm gods; the Letoon sanctuary of Leto, Apollo and Artemis served all Lycia
entries.fell_by: Persian rule, then Alexander; annexed by Rome in 43 CE as Lycia et Pamphylia
entries.notes: Their federal Lycian League was cited by Madison in Federalist no. 9 as a model for the US Constitution.

entries.name: Cypriots
subsistence: copper mining (the island gave the metal its name)
entries.settlement: ten, later seven, Greek and Phoenician city-kingdoms (Salamis, Kition, Paphos)
entries.beliefs: Aphrodite, born at Paphos, and Phoenician Astarte; cults of the city-kings
entries.fell_by: Assyrian tribute, Persian rule, then Alexander; annexed to Rome by Ptolemy in 58 BCE
entries.notes: Copper was so tied to the island that its name is still the Latin word for it: cuprum.

entries.name: Arameans
entries.settlement: small city-states (Damascus, Arpad, Hamath) of farmers and caravan-minders
crafts: the Aramaic alphabet, lingua franca of the Near East
trade: caravans linking Mesopotamia with the Levant and Anatolia
entries.beliefs: Hadad, the storm god, and Atargatis, the fish-goddess; ancestor cults
entries.fell_by: Assyrian conquest of the Aramean city-states by 732 BCE; Aramaic outlived them as the Near East's tongue
entries.notes: Almost everyone in the Persian empire spoke Aramaic; Jesus of Nazareth likely prayed in it.

entries.name: Judeans
entries.settlement: Jerusalem-centred petty kingdom, then the province of Judea under successive empires; the Second Temple rebuilt 516 BCE
crafts: scribal literacy in Hebrew and Aramaic
entries.beliefs: monotheism - Yahweh alone; Torah law; Temple sacrifice, then rabbinic Judaism after 70 CE
entries.fell_by: Babylonian exile (586 BCE), Roman destruction of the Temple (70 CE), and the Bar Kokhba revolt (135 CE)
entries.notes: The smallest people to rewrite world history; their scriptures remain half the Christian Bible.

entries.name: Nabataeans
entries.settlement: caravan cities (Petra, Hegra) carved into sandstone; a relay network across the Hejaz and Negev
entries.beliefs: Dushara, the lord of the mountain, and al-'Uzza; block-stone and ancestor cults
entries.fell_by: annexed by Rome in 106 CE as Provincia Arabia; sea trade drained the caravans and Petra declined
entries.notes: Petra's Treasury is only a facade; the real marvel is their desert agriculture - water caught from flash floods.

entries.name: Palmyrenes
entries.settlement: an oasis caravan city; semi-autonomous under Rome, partner of empires east and west
crafts: caravan brokerage of the silk roads
entries.beliefs: Bel's temple fuses Mesopotamian and Greek rites; proud ancestor worship in portrait busts
entries.fell_by: Zenobia seized power in the East; Emperor Aurelian stormed and sacked Palmyra in 273 CE
entries.notes: Queen Zenobia's short-lived empire stretched from Egypt to Anatolia; the city never recovered its trade.

entries.name: Tartessians
subsistence: tin, copper and silver mining (Rio Tinto)
entries.settlement: a wealthy trading kingdom around the city of Tartessos (probably Huelva) - semi-mythical to Greek authors
entries.beliefs: Astarte (Potnia) and Baal (Melqart) after Phoenician contact; sanctuaries at Castulo and Carmona
entries.fell_by: absorbed into Classic Iberian culture by 500 BCE; most sites were inexplicably abandoned in the 5th century
entries.notes: Greek writers called them the richest people west of the Straits; they may be the seed of Plato's Atlantis tale. Their language is untouched.

entries.name: Numidians
entries.settlement: a Berber kingdom of tribes fused by a royal dynasty (Massinissa); capitals Siga, then Cirta
entries.beliefs: Berber gods and ancestor cults; royal tombs such as the Medracen
entries.fell_by: Jugurthine War against Rome (112-106 BCE); Juba I lost at Thapsus (46 BCE); Numidia became Roman provinces
entries.notes: Their fast horsemen decided most wars in Africa; even Hannibal begged for them.

entries.name: Nuragic Sardinians
entries.settlement: villages clustered around nuraghi - some 7000 tower-fortresses survive across the island
entries.beliefs: a bull cult and water sanctuaries; ancestor tombs ('giants' graves')
entries.fell_by: Punic occupation, then final Roman conquest in 238 BCE after the First Punic War
entries.notes: Their towers make Sardinia one of Europe's megalithic heartlands; what a nuraghe was for is still debated.

entries.name: Talayotic Balearics
entries.settlement: stone tower (talayot) settlements ringed around fertile land; megalithic sanctuaries (taules, navetas)
crafts: sling-warfare training (their slingers were universal mercenaries)
entries.beliefs: a bull cult glimpsed in the taula sanctuaries; the dead laid in navetas shaped like inverted ships
entries.fell_by: Quintus Metellus's expedition of 123 BCE; the Balearics became a Roman province
entries.notes: Hannibal paid for their slingers, and Romans learned at sieges like Carthage why; they were the best missile troops of the ancient world.

entries.name: Aquitanians
entries.region: Southwest Gaul (Aquitaine, foothills of the Pyrenees)
entries.settlement: small oppida and open farms; speaking a language distinct from Gaulish - Proto-Basque
entries.beliefs: mountain and sky gods ancestral to the Basque pantheon; healing-spring sanctuaries
entries.fell_by: Caesar's campaign of 56 BCE; their language survived in the Pyrenees and became Basque
entries.notes: The last pre-Indo-European language in Western Europe - Basque - descends from theirs.

entries.name: Garamantians
subsistence: trans-Saharan trade - gold, ivory, slaves, ostrich feathers
entries.settlement: a dozen oasis towns fed by thousands of foggaras; capital Garama (Jerma); perhaps 30,000 people
entries.beliefs: Berber ancestor and water spirits; a script existed but almost nothing is legible
entries.fell_by: Islamic-era conversion and the foggaras silting up; the oases withered by the 10th century
entries.notes: They farmed hyper-arid desert with tunnel irrigation centuries ahead of anyone else; Herodotus describes them hunting cave-dwellers from chariots.

entries.name: Urartians
entries.region: Lake Van region (eastern Anatolia and Armenia)
entries.settlement: a fortress kingdom centred on the Van rock citadel, Tushpa; a ring of mountain strongholds
crafts: bronze shields and helmets with geometric friezes
entries.beliefs: Haldi the war-god, with Teisheba (storm) and Shivini (sun); Haldi's temples anchored every citadel
entries.fell_by: Scythian raids and the Medes; the kingdom was wiped off the map c. 610-590 BCE
entries.notes: Their canals still water the Ararat plain; they are the ancestors of the Armenians and rival of Assyria.
